title: Leading at the Rock Face
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that the only way for a leader to genuinely understand their organization's customer experience is to become the customer, not merely study or interview one. Using an airline executive as a running example — booking a ticket, checking a bag, standing in security, sitting in a coach seat — the piece shows how full immersion surfaces frustrations and assumptions that surveys and focus groups can't reach. It generalizes the idea across professions (teachers becoming students, pastors becoming parishioners, engineers becoming end-users) and argues the exercise is valuable precisely because it's uncomfortable: it forces leaders to confront how different their own experience is from the people they serve.
points: The central claim is that becoming a customer, not just studying one, is the only reliable way for a leader to understand their organization's real end-user experience.
The airline executive example (booking, checking in, security, coach seating) is used to show how full immersion surfaces friction that surveys and focus groups miss.
The practice is generalized across professions — teachers becoming students, doctors becoming patients, salespeople becoming buyers — as a repeatable leadership discipline.
The piece frames the discomfort of the exercise as the point: leading at the rock face reveals how different a leader's own experience is from that of the people the organization actually serves.
quotes: When leaders sit where customers sit, do what customers do, and experience what customers experience, they finally begin to understand what their organization does.
Leading at the rock face means becoming physically and personally connected to your enterprise in the same way a customer does.
Nothing short of that complete experience can compare to what a leader might learn about the company and how it works or doesn’t.
Good leaders in all walks of life can choose to lead at the rock face: Teachers can become students, coaches can become players, pastors can become parishioners.
As a customer, leaders learn firsthand what needs to be improved, amplified, or corrected.
From the vantage of a customer, leading at the rock face is both reassuring and scary.
